articles.headline: OFAC Designates Entities and Individuals in Latest Iran-Related Action
body: The U.S. Department of the Treasury's Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced new Iran-related designations on November 23, 2026. This action is part of ongoing efforts to counter the Iranian regime's activities.

The specifics of the designated entities and individuals were not immediately detailed in the initial announcement but are expected to target those involved in supporting Iran's illicit financial activities or its proliferation efforts. These designations aim to further isolate Iran from the international financial system.

This action follows a series of recent Iran-related designations and updates by OFAC, underscoring a continued focus on disrupting networks that provide revenue and support for the Iranian government.

articles.headline: OFAC Issues New Iran Designations and Cuba FAQs
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced new Iran designations and the issuance of Cuba Frequently Asked Questions (FAQs) on November 20, 2026. This dual action addresses ongoing concerns regarding both Iran's illicit activities and the implementation of sanctions against Cuba.

The Iran designations target individuals and entities involved in oil sales and sanctions evasion, with four Iranian nationals identified as intermediaries collecting proceeds from Iranian oil sales abroad. Mojtaba Arabnejad, Mohammad Javad Bavand, Mohammadhossein Servati, and Majid Taj were sanctioned, with Arabnejad linked to Mahan Air and Servati to Sepehr Energy Jahan Nama Pars Company under counterterrorism authorities. Bavand and Taj were sanctioned under Executive Order 13902, which targets individuals and entities operating in designated sectors of Iran's economy.

In addition to the Iran-related actions, OFAC also issued new FAQs concerning Cuba, providing guidance on existing regulations and potentially clarifying aspects of the expanded U.S. sanctions targeting the Cuban economy under Executive Order 14404.

articles.headline: OFAC Imposes Counter Narcotics and Cyber Sanctions, Amends Russia GL
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced a series of actions on November 19, 2026, including new counter narcotics and cyber-related designations. These measures aim to disrupt illicit activities that pose threats to U.S. national security.

Alongside these designations, OFAC issued an Illicit Drugs General License, providing authorizations for certain transactions related to illicit drug interdiction efforts. This license aims to facilitate legitimate activities while maintaining pressure on criminal organizations.

Furthermore, OFAC issued an amended Russia-related General License and updated Frequently Asked Questions. This amendment likely provides clarifications or adjustments to existing sanctions on Russia, reflecting the evolving geopolitical landscape and ongoing efforts to counter Russian aggression.

articles.headline: OFAC Announces New Counter Terrorism Designations
body: The U.S. Department of the Treasury's Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) implemented new counter terrorism designations on November 18, 2026. These actions are part of the ongoing global effort to combat terrorism financing and disrupt terrorist networks.

The designations target individuals and entities found to be providing material support, financial, or technological services to terrorist organizations. The specific details of those designated were not immediately released but are expected to be published on the OFAC website.
These measures aim to freeze assets and prohibit U.S. persons from engaging in transactions with the designated parties, thereby limiting their ability to fund and carry out terrorist activities.

articles.headline: OFAC Targets Narcotics and Terrorism with New Designations
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced new designations on November 13, 2026, targeting individuals and entities involved in both counter narcotics and counter terrorism activities. This action highlights the interconnectedness of these illicit networks.

These designations aim to disrupt the financial and operational capabilities of organizations and individuals that engage in drug trafficking and support terrorist groups. The specific targets were not immediately identified in the initial announcement.

The U.S. government continues to leverage its sanctions authorities to combat these threats, working to safeguard the international financial system from abuse by criminal and terrorist organizations.

articles.headline: OFAC Publishes Iran Designation Update
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) issued an Iran Designation Update on November 9, 2026. This update likely involves modifications or additions to existing designations related to Iran.

Such updates can include the identification of new aliases for previously sanctioned entities, changes in identifying information, or the addition of new entities or individuals to the sanctions list. These adjustments are crucial for maintaining the effectiveness of the sanctions regime.

The continuous updating of designation information helps financial institutions and other regulated entities to comply with sanctions requirements and prevent illicit transactions involving sanctioned parties.

articles.headline: OFAC Implements New Iran-Related Designations
body: The U.S. Department of the Treasury's Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced new Iran-related designations on November 6, 2026. This action is part of the ongoing U.S. strategy to exert economic pressure on the Iranian regime.

These designations typically target individuals, entities, and vessels involved in various sectors of the Iranian economy, including those supporting its nuclear program, ballistic missile development, or regional destabilizing activities.
The aim of these measures is to disrupt Iran's ability to generate revenue and acquire resources for its illicit activities, reinforcing the comprehensive sanctions framework against the country.

articles.headline: OFAC Designates Cyber and Transnational Criminal Organizations, Imposes Cuba Sanctions
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced significant actions on November 5, 2026, including new cyber-related and transnational criminal organizations designations, as well as Cuba designations and the publication of a Cuba-related determination.

OFAC imposed blocking sanctions against five individuals and 41 entities supporting global scam networks, with four individuals and 41 entities targeted under the transnational criminal organizations authority for supporting or operating within Prince Group's corporate and financial network. Additionally, OFAC designated Chui Kok Wa, a Malaysian national, under its cyber sanctions authority for leading scammers who defrauded U.S. victims.

Regarding Cuba, OFAC added two individuals, six entities, and two vessels to the SDN List under E.O. 14404, with individuals listed in Cuba and Panama and entities in Cuba, China, and Panama. A separate determination, effective November 5, extends the order's sectoral designation authority to Cuba's electronics, manufacturing, marine, and technology sectors, providing a basis for designating foreign persons operating in those sectors.

articles.headline: OFAC Issues Iran-Related Designations, Updates, and Venezuela GL Amendment
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced new Iran-related designations, updates to certain Iran-related listings, and the publication of an Iran-related OFAC Alert on November 4, 2026. These actions reinforce the U.S. government's commitment to countering Iran's destabilizing activities.

The Iran-related designations and updates aim to enhance the effectiveness of existing sanctions by targeting new avenues of evasion or identifying additional entities supporting the Iranian regime. The OFAC Alert provides guidance to the public on potential risks and compliance obligations.

Additionally, OFAC issued an amended Venezuela-related General License and Frequently Asked Question. This amendment likely provides adjustments or clarifications to existing sanctions on Venezuela, reflecting ongoing policy considerations.

articles.headline: OFAC Issues Amended Iran-Related General License
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) issued an amended Iran-related General License on October 29, 2026. This amendment modifies existing authorizations for certain transactions involving Iran.

General Licenses are issued to authorize categories of transactions that would otherwise be prohibited by sanctions. Amendments can expand, narrow, or clarify the scope of permitted activities, often in response to evolving policy considerations or humanitarian concerns.
Entities engaging in Iran-related activities should review the amended General License carefully to ensure ongoing compliance with U.S. sanctions regulations.

articles.headline: Addressing Remote Access to Advanced Semiconductors
body: In this interim final rule (IFR), the Department of Commerce is establishing new rules to prevent certain foreign actors from leveraging advanced computing power based on U.S. technology to threaten U.S. national security and foreign policy interests. First, this rule establishes new restrictions which will apply for exports, reexports, or transfers (in-country) to overseas data centers that remotely supply significant volumes of compute to companies headquartered in Country Group D:5 or Macau. These restrictions will undermine the ability of companies headquartered in countries of concern from using U.S. advanced Super Intelligence (SI) semiconductors to train advanced SI models. Data centers, foreign foundries, and chip exporters are required to perform robust due diligence on their customers, including any direct or indirect ownership or control by persons in Country Group D:5 or Macau, as part of complying with this new control. The license requirement will not apply to commercial recommender systems, such as those used by online retailers or social media companies, as these functions do not pose the same national security threat. Second, in addition to the current license requirements for advanced semiconductors, a license will be required to export, reexport, or transfer (in-country) advanced semiconductors to Indonesia, Malaysia, Singapore, Thailand, or Brazil (and any additional country designated by the Secretary of Commerce, in consultation with the Secretary of State or the Assistant to the President for National Security Affairs)--countries which present a higher-than-normal risk of diversion. The license requirement for these five countries will not apply to semiconductors destined to companies headquartered in, or whose ultimate parent company is headquartered in, the United States, provided certain reporting requirements are met. Commerce will be actively monitoring for countries that tolerate evasion of this IFR and will consider a range of consequences for such countries, such as import restrictions, new license requirements on advanced semiconductor exports, downgrading the country's status in the U.S. export control regime, and Entity List designations and temporary export prohibitions for foreign persons involved in such activities. Third, this IFR amends the presumptions which front-end chips fabricators and chip packagers face when exporting advanced-node logic chips. These amendments reduce the number of pathways to overcome the presumptions for chip designers located in destinations which face a license requirement for SI chips. This change gives the U.S. government critical oversight over companies headquartered in certain countries that seek to leverage advanced semiconductor production capabilities in third countries. Finally, the IFR formally rescinds the regulations implementing the Biden-era AI Diffusion Rule. The AI Diffusion Rule has never been enforced. The regulatory changes in this rule formalize the rescission of the AI Diffusion Rule, which the Department of Commerce Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) announced in May 2025.

articles.headline: Streamlining Export Controls for Drone Exports
body: The Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) is easing export controls on certain Unmanned Aerial Vehicles (UAVs or drones) and related parts, components, accessories, attachments, technology, and software under the Export Administration Regulations (EAR). Specifically, this rule: eliminates wind gust tolerance as a parameter for determining UAV controls under the EAR; increases the threshold for national security controls on certain UAVs from an endurance of 30 minutes to an endurance of 3 hours; makes conforming changes to remove national security controls on software and technology associated with UAVs with an endurance less than 3 hours; maintains military end-use and end-user controls on those lower endurance drones and associated software and technology; clarifies Commerce Control List (CCL) controls for certain UAVs specially designed for military use; and removes national security controls on certain specially designed parts, components, accessories, and attachments for such UAVs as they do not provide any significant military or intelligence capabilities.

articles.headline: Democrats win largest House majority since 1992 after flipping North Carolina seat
body: Democrats have now won at least 258 seats in the midterms compared to Republicans, who hold at least 173 seats.

articles.headline: US Army to detonate tonnes of unstable explosives in Iowa despite court order
body: The Army says "swift action" is necessary to protect its personnel and nearby communities around its ammunition plant in Iowa.

articles.headline: Three killed and dozens missing after fire at Indonesian factory
body: At least three people were killed and many more feared dead after a fire at a confectionary factory.

articles.headline: Mexican drug lord on FBI's 10 most wanted list arrested in shoot-out
body: Fausto Isidro "Chapo Idisro" Meza Flores, who is accused of drug trafficking and torture, is detained after gun fight with authorities.

articles.headline: Italian jeweller and businessman Paolo Bulgari dies aged 89
body: In a statement to Italian media, his family remember him as "the greatest jeweller of our time".

articles.headline: FBI reportedly investigating apparent hack of its criminal database
body: The National Crime Information Center database is used by federal and local law enforcement to share information.
